problem.text: How many ordered pairs of real numbers $(x,y)$ satisfy the following system of equations? $$\begin{aligned} x+3y&=3 \\ \big|\,|x|-|y|\,\big|&=1 \end{aligned}$$

steps.title: Where to start: use the line to remove $x$
steps.body: The first equation is a plain line, so solve it for $x$: $x = 3 - 3y$. Now everything depends on $y$ alone. The absolute values are the hard part, and they only change form when $x$ or $y$ changes sign.

your_turn.prompt: For which values of $y$ is $x = 3 - 3y$ at least $0$?

steps.title: Split into three ranges of $y$
steps.body: The sign of $y$ changes at $0$ and the sign of $x$ changes at $y = 1$. So check three ranges: $y < 0$, then $0 \le y \le 1$, then $y > 1$. In each range, write $|x| - |y|$ without absolute values and set it equal to $\pm 1$. For $y < 0$, $|x| - |y| = (3 - 3y) - (-y) = 3 - 2y$.

your_turn.prompt: Solve $3 - 2y = 1$ and $3 - 2y = -1$. Do the answers fit $y < 0$?
your_turn.answer: $y = 1$ and $y = 2$. Neither is negative, so this range gives no solutions.

steps.title: Check the other two ranges
steps.body: For $0 \le y \le 1$, both $x$ and $y$ are nonnegative, so $|x| - |y| = 3 - 4y$. For $y > 1$, $x$ is negative, so $|x| - |y| = (3y - 3) - y = 2y - 3$. Solve each for $\pm 1$ and keep only the answers inside the range.

your_turn.prompt: Solve $3 - 4y = 1$ and $3 - 4y = -1$. Which answers satisfy $0 \le y \le 1$?

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: In the last range, $2y - 3 = 1$ gives $y = 2$, which is allowed, while $2y - 3 = -1$ gives $y = 1$, which is not greater than $1$, so it is thrown out. Careful: $y = 1$ came up as a candidate in two ranges where it does not belong; it counts only once, as the point $(0, 1)$ from the middle range. The solutions are $(\frac{3}{2}, \frac{1}{2})$, $(0, 1)$ and $(-3, 2)$, and each one checks in both equations. That gives $3$ ordered pairs. The answer is **(C)**.

wrong_choices.D: $4$ comes from handling the first two ranges correctly but slipping in the last one: in the range $y > 1$, the equation $2y - 3 = -1$ gives $y = 1$, and keeping it adds the point $(0, 1)$ a second time. But $y = 1$ is not greater than $1$, so it does not belong to that range, and it is the same point already found in the middle range anyway.

verification.verifier_notes: Hole found by adversarial verifier, fixed twice, and re-verified by a fresh verifier.
